articles.title: Can music change what guests order?
articles.desc: Not how much guests spend, but what they choose: what field and lab studies found about music, volume, genre and the order itself.
articles.author: SensEar Team
articles.alt: Black-and-white photo of a couple sipping frozen cocktails through straws on a wicker sofa

structuredContent.value: Quick take
Our earlier post looked at how music changes how long guests stay and how much they spend. This one asks a narrower question: can music change which dish, drink or bottle a guest picks?

The answer from the research is yes, in three specific ways. Music that signals a country steers guests towards that country's food and wine. Lower volume steers them towards lighter, healthier options. And music genre nudges the choice between healthy and indulgent, and between savoury and sweet. The effects are measurable, but they work best when the music fits what the menu already offers.
Three routes from the speaker to the order
The first route is origin. Music carries a flag. When a track sounds French, Italian or Greek, the matching dishes feel like the natural choice. Guests rarely notice this happening.

The second route is arousal. Louder music raises energy and lowers self-control, which favours indulgent choices. Quieter music relaxes people, which favours lighter choices ([Biswas, Lund & Szocs, 2019](https://doi.org/10.1007/s11747-018-0583-8)).

The third route is association. Genres carry meanings. Classical music reads as refined and sweet, jazz as relaxed, rock and hip-hop as energetic. Those meanings carry over to the food in front of the guest ([Motoki, Takahashi, Velasco & Spence, 2021](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.foodqual.2021.104380)).
What the research found

items: The wine aisle study. In a British supermarket, French and German wines sat side by side with flags on the shelf. On days with French music, French wine outsold German by about five to one. On days with German music, German wine outsold French by about two to one. Most shoppers said the music had not influenced them ([North, Hargreaves & McKendrick, 1997](https://doi.org/10.1038/36484)).

Paella or chicken parmesan. In a university dining hall, Spanish music doubled the share of diners choosing seafood paella, from 17% to 34%, compared with nights when Italian music played. The music changed the choice but not how much people liked the dish once they ate it ([Zellner et al., 2017](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.foodqual.2016.10.004)).

Volume and healthy sales. In a café and a supermarket, lower-volume music and noise increased sales of healthy items, while higher volume raised the share of unhealthy items. The explanation was relaxation: calmer guests made lighter choices ([Biswas, Lund & Szocs, 2019](https://doi.org/10.1007/s11747-018-0583-8)).

A "healthy soundtrack". Researchers first asked people in China and Denmark which sounds matched healthy and unhealthy eating. They then built two soundtracks: a slow, high-pitched jazz piano piece and a fast, low-pitched, dissonant guitar piece. Participants who heard the jazz piece chose fruit and vegetables more often; those who heard the guitar piece chose pizza and doughnuts more often ([Peng-Li et al., 2021](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.appet.2021.105264)).

Genre and the menu. In two experiments with almost 800 participants, jazz and classical music increased preference for healthy savoury dishes such as a vegetable sandwich. Rock, hip-hop and jazz increased preference for indulgent savoury dishes such as a beef sandwich. Classical music increased preference for sweet foods, both the healthier and the indulgent kind ([Motoki et al., 2021](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.foodqual.2021.104380)).

Classical and the price of the bottle. In a wine shop, classical music (compared with chart pop) led customers to buy more expensive wines ([Areni & Kim, 1993](https://ro.uow.edu.au/gsbpapers/462), cited in Motoki et al., 2021).

structuredContent.value: Where it stops working

Some of these studies were run online or in a lab, with pictures of food rather than real plates. The genre study, for example, measured stated preference, not sales, and the authors say so themselves.
Results on genre are not uniform. One earlier study found no effect of genre on healthy choices at all. What held up across studies was volume and origin, not every genre claim.

And music changes the choice, not the pleasure. In the dining-hall study, guests who picked paella because of the music did not enjoy it more than guests who picked it on a quiet night. Music can open the door to a dish. The kitchen still has to deliver it.
What this means for restaurants, bars and hotels

Start with the menu, not the playlist. If you run a taverna or a meze restaurant built around Greek produce and recipes, Greek-rooted music supports every order that depends on it. If the wine list leans French or Italian, a few hours a week with music from those places is a low-cost test.

For a wellness hotel, a healthy breakfast buffet or a lunch spot with a light menu, volume matters more than genre. The research points to calmer, quieter sound and towards jazz and classical rather than loud, dense music. This is one of the few places where the science and the brand concept pull in the same direction.

For a pastry counter, a dessert course or a cocktail bar with a sweet-forward list, classical and other consonant, higher-pitched music gives the sweet options a push. For a bar with a bold, savoury menu and a late crowd, energetic genres fit the food as well as the hour.
For a wine list with premium bottles, the oldest finding in this area still applies: classical music helps guests feel that the better bottle is the right choice.
The SensEar checklist: music that supports the menu

items: Write down what you most want guests to order. The dish with the best margin, the house wine, the dessert. Music should support that list, not fight it.
Match origin where it is honest. Music from the same place as the food supports the order. Music from a place the menu has nothing to do with sends a mixed signal.
Use volume as a dial for the menu, not only for the mood. Lighter menu, lower volume. Richer menu, a notch more energy.
Think in dayparts. Breakfast and lunch can lean calm and acoustic; the late shift can lean energetic. The menu changes across the day and the music should follow it.
Do not expect music to fix a weak dish. The studies show music changes the pick, not the rating. Quality still decides whether they come back.
Test with one metric. Pick one item, change only the music for two matched weeks, and count how often it is ordered.

articles.title: Music as a filter: who walks in, who walks out
articles.desc: Every soundtrack lets some people in and keeps others out. How volume, genre and familiarity work as filters, and when a filter starts to cost you.
articles.author: SensEar Team
articles.alt: A couple in bold 1980s nightlife outfits laughing in front of a red curtain

structuredContent.value: Quick take

There is no neutral playlist. Every choice of music tells some people "this is for you" and tells others "this is not". Most venues make that choice by accident. A few make it on purpose, and the clearest case is a clothing shop that turned its music up to nightclub level to keep the wrong customers out.

The lesson is not "be loud". The lesson is that volume, genre and familiarity each work as a filter, that a filter can be a strength, and that a filter built for one audience can quietly turn against you when the audience moves on.
The loudest shop in the mall

Abercrombie & Fitch sold to 15 to 28 year olds and said so in its music policy: music first, merchandise second. The brand avoided radio hits and picked artists a college student might know but the mainstream did not yet. Then it played them loud.

That was deliberate. In a Portland store, an observer measured 90 decibels on the floor and up to 98 near the speakers, and watched shoppers turn around at the door or leave within minutes. Television crews in two US cities measured 85 and 90 decibels in the same chain, levels an audiologist in one report described as hazardous over a full working day ([Deseret News, 2012](https://www.deseret.com/2012/11/6/20509358/shopping-out-loud-retail-stores-getting-noisier-to-stimulate-more-purchases-study-says)).

For the target customer, the same volume created a club feeling and a sense of belonging. For everyone else, it created an exit. A widely quoted New York Times piece from 2012 described a grandmother in one of the stores who said ten minutes felt like an hour and that she would buy anything just to leave. A meta-analysis of retail music studies confirms the pattern: louder music shortens the time people spend in a store ([Garlin & Owen, 2006](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0148296306000282)).

Then the audience changed. In May 2014, after eight straight quarters of falling same-store sales, the company announced it would turn the music down, turn the lights up, ease off the fragrance and take the shirtless models off the walls ([CBS News, 2014](https://www.cbsnews.com/amp/news/abercrombie-learns-some-hard-retail-lessons)). The filter had not stopped working. It had kept working on a customer who was no longer the one the brand needed.
Why music filters people

Music is one of the strongest signals of who we are. In a landmark study, music preferences fell into four broad families: reflective and complex, intense and rebellious, upbeat and conventional, energetic and rhythmic. Each family lined up with personality traits ([Rentfrow & Gosling, 2003](https://doi.org/10.1037/0022-3514.84.6.1236)).

A follow-up study found that music was the single most common topic when strangers got to know each other, and that people could judge a stranger's personality from their music preferences with real accuracy ([Rentfrow & Gosling, 2006](https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1467-9280.2006.01691.x)).

A venue's soundtrack works the same way in reverse. Guests read the music and decide, within seconds, whether this is a place for people like them. Earlier research pointed in the same direction: extroverts leaned towards rock and louder, more emotional music, while more introverted people leaned towards calmer and more structured music.
Three filters, three different costs

Volume is the hard filter. It works on the body, not on taste. Above conversation level, guests who did not come for the music leave sooner, whatever genre is playing. It is the easiest filter to apply and the most expensive to get wrong.

Genre is the identity filter. A rebetiko night, a techno set and a jazz trio each call a different crowd. This filter is strong and cheap, but it is only as good as your knowledge of who you want in the room and who you can afford to lose.

Familiarity is the soft filter. Abercrombie chose artists its audience half-knew. Music that is slightly ahead of what guests already listen to creates curiosity and a feeling of being in the know. Music that is far ahead of them creates distance. Music that is far behind them, or on every radio, creates nothing at all.
When a filter is a strength, and when it starts to cost

A filter is a strength when three things are true: you serve one clear audience, visits are short, and the people you keep out would not have spent much anyway. A late-night bar, a concept store, a members' club.

A filter starts to cost when the room is mixed. A hotel lobby serves a couple on honeymoon, a family with a grandmother and a consultant on a laptop in the same hour. A restaurant on a Greek island serves locals at one table and visitors from four countries at the next. In these rooms, a hard filter does not sharpen the brand. It sends paying guests to the competitor across the street.
And a filter costs most when the audience moves on and the music does not. Abercrombie's customers grew up, and the brand kept playing to the ones who had left.
What this means for hotels, restaurants and bars

Decide first who the room is for, by hour. A beach bar at six in the evening and the same bar at midnight are two different rooms with two different audiences. Dayparting is a soft filter: it lets you welcome families early and shift the mood later without a sign on the door.

Use volume last, not first. If you want a younger, high-energy crowd, build it with genre, familiarity and timing before you reach for the volume. Volume filters by force, and it filters your staff as well as your guests.

In mixed rooms, filter by energy, not by identity. A hotel lobby or an all-day restaurant can hold a clear character without picking a tribe. Consistent energy, consistent quality and a sound that fits the space keep the character while leaving the door open.

Review the filter once a year. Ask who is in the room now, who you want in it next year, and whether the music still speaks to them. The most dangerous playlist is the one that worked three years ago.
The SensEar checklist: a filter you choose

items: Write down who the music is for, by daypart. If the answer is "everyone", you have no filter and probably no character either.
Write down who it is allowed to keep out. If that list includes families, older guests or hotel residents, check that the money adds up.
Measure the volume at the tables, not at the bar. Conversation should not need a raised voice unless that is the explicit point of the room, and only after midnight.
Use genre and familiarity before volume. They filter by taste, which guests forgive. Volume filters by force, which they do not.
Look at the room, not the playlist. Count who leaves within ten minutes and who stays an hour. That is the filter working, for better or worse.
Revisit the filter every season. Audiences move, and a sound built for last year's crowd is the Abercrombie mistake in slow motion.

articles.title: Why familiar music sells: recognition and brand memory
articles.desc: People choose what they recognise. What research on music recognition, mere exposure and brand recall means for the sound of a venue.
articles.author: SensEar Team
articles.alt: Illustration of a woman in white scattering stars above a city skyline at night

structuredContent.value: Quick take

An earlier post looked at music that fits a brand. This one looks at music that people recognise. The two are not the same. A track can fit your venue perfectly and be new to every guest, or be known to everyone and fit nothing.

Recognition has its own effect. In two experiments with 486 people, unknown brands were chosen more often when they came with music the participants had heard before. The same study found something a venue should care about even more: whether people liked the music mattered more than whether they recognised it, and music they strongly disliked cancelled the benefit ([Anglada-Tort et al., 2022](https://doi.org/10.1080/02650487.2022.2060568)).
Two old ideas behind a new finding

The first idea is mere exposure. People come to prefer things simply because they have met them before, even when they do not remember the meeting. Psychologists have tested this since the 1960s ([Zajonc, 1968](https://doi.org/10.1037/h0025848)).

The second idea is the recognition shortcut. When people must choose between two options and know only one of them, they tend to pick the one they know. They treat recognition as a sign of quality, because checking properly would take time they do not have ([Goldstein & Gigerenzer, 2002](https://doi.org/10.1037/0033-295X.109.1.75)).
Music is a strong trigger for both. People recognise a familiar song within a second or two, long before they could say where they heard it.
What the research found

items: Recognised music tipped the choice. Participants first learned a set of short music clips. They then chose between pairs of real but unknown brands of headphones, cameras, tennis racquets and phones. Each brand appeared with an eight-second clip, one learned and one new. Brands with the recognised clip were chosen 59% of the time in the first experiment and 56% in the second ([Anglada-Tort et al., 2022](https://doi.org/10.1080/02650487.2022.2060568)).
The honest size of the effect is six points. The authors use the lower figure: recognised music moved choice from the 50% you would expect by chance to 56%. That is a small effect, and a real one.

Liking mattered more. When the researchers added how much each person liked each clip, liking had a clearly larger effect on choice than recognition did. Recognition added to liking across most of the scale.
Disliked music cancelled the benefit. For the clips people disliked most, recognition stopped helping, and those brands were chosen least of all.

Familiarity has a ceiling. A review of 57 studies on music preference found that 50 of them fit the same curve: liking rises as music becomes familiar, then falls when it becomes too familiar ([Chmiel & Schubert, 2017](https://doi.org/10.1177/0305735617697507)).

People remember brands through different parts of the music. A small survey study of advertising music sorted listeners into four types: those who remember through lyrics, those who need the music to fit the message, those who respond to a familiar tune or voice, and those who respond to soft music ([Iyer & Aggarwal, 2019](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/336982994)).

structuredContent.value: Where it stops working

The main study was an online experiment about advertising, not a field test in a venue. People chose between brands they had never heard of, with nothing else to go on. In real life they have prices, reviews and friends' opinions, so the effect will usually be smaller.
Recognition and liking were also tangled together. People tend to like what they know, and the authors say plainly that their design could not fully separate the two.

And recognition is not the same as popularity. The clips in the study were not hits. They were unknown songs that participants had learned minutes earlier. What helped was that the listener had met the music before, not that the music was famous.
What this means for hotels, restaurants and bars
There are two ways a venue can use recognition, and they pull in different directions.

The first is borrowed recognition: playing music guests already know. It gives a room instant warmth and lowers the effort of being somewhere new. It also has a cost. If every track is a hit, your venue sounds like every other venue, and the music is recognised but you are not. The ceiling applies too: the songs guests hear everywhere are the first ones they tire of.

The second is owned recognition: becoming the thing that is recognised. A venue with a consistent sound, heard on every visit, builds its own mere exposure effect. Guests may not name a single track, but they know the place by ear. The same applies outside the room. If your videos, your events and your phone line carry the same musical character as your terrace, each contact makes the next one more familiar.

For most venues the answer is a mix. Use a small number of familiar anchors to make the room easy to enter, and build the rest from music that fits and that guests will come to recognise as yours. The study's second finding sets the limit: a familiar track that your guests dislike does more harm than an unknown track they enjoy.
The SensEar checklist: recognition that works for you

items: Ask "familiar to whom?". Familiar means known to your guests, not known to the charts. A track that every local knows may be new to your summer visitors, and the reverse.
Use familiar tracks as anchors, not as the whole programme. Place them where a room needs warmth: the first hour, a slow afternoon, the moment a new group walks in.
Put liking first. If you are unsure whether guests enjoy a familiar track, leave it out. The research is clear that disliked music cancels the benefit of recognition.
Rotate before the ceiling. Liking falls when music becomes too familiar, and your staff reach that point long before your guests do.
Build a sound guests can recognise as yours. Keep the same character across visits, across spaces and across the year, even as the tracks change.

Carry that sound outside the room. Use the same musical character in videos, events and on hold. Note that a well-known song in a video or an advert needs its own licence, separate from the licence for the venue.
Check it with returning guests. Ask a few of them how they would describe the music of the place. If they can answer, recognition is working.

articles.title: Beyond sound: when music, light, scent and temperature agree
articles.desc: Guests do not hear, see and smell a venue separately. What research shows about matched and clashing cues, and how to check your own space.
articles.author: SensEar Team
articles.alt: Woman in a white dress on a seaside terrace with a white cockatoo and two macaws

structuredContent.value: Quick take

Guests do not experience a venue one sense at a time. They do not hear the music, then notice the light, then smell the air. The brain combines everything into one impression within seconds, and that impression is what they remember.

Research on this has a clear message. When the cues agree, they reinforce each other. When they clash, the result can be worse than using only one cue. In one study, a Christmas scent paired with the wrong music made a shop look less attractive, not more ([Spangenberg, Grohmann & Sprott, 2005](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0148296304002000)).

Most venues design each sense separately. An architect sets the light, a supplier installs a scent diffuser, a manager picks the music and maintenance sets the thermostat. Nobody checks whether the four agree.
One room, one impression

Researchers who study shops describe the environment as a whole that people judge at once. A useful way to think about it is energy. Light, music, scent and temperature each push guests towards calm or towards alertness. When they all push in the same direction, the effect is stronger. When they push in opposite directions, guests feel that something is off without knowing why ([Mattila & Wirtz, 2001](https://doi.org/10.1016/S0022-4359(01)00042-2)).

Aradhna Krishna, who runs the Sensory Marketing Laboratory at the University of Michigan, puts it simply: the senses amplify one another when they are congruent. Her own example is a heating pad that seemed to work better when it smelled of cinnamon, because cinnamon suggests warmth ([Harvard Business Review, 2015](https://hbr.org/2015/03/the-science-of-sensory-marketing)).
What the research found

items: Matched energy worked better than either cue alone. In a field study in a store, researchers combined three music conditions with three scent conditions. When the energy of the scent matched the energy of the music, shoppers rated the store more positively, showed more approach behaviour, bought more on impulse and reported higher satisfaction ([Mattila & Wirtz, 2001](https://doi.org/10.1016/S0022-4359(01)00042-2)).

Half a theme can hurt. In a mock store, shoppers rated the store well when Christmas music and a Christmas scent were used together. When one festive cue appeared without the other, ratings fell below those of a store with no festive cues at all. Even the full theme did no better than no theme. The authors' own advice was blunt: if you cannot make two cues agree, use only one ([Spangenberg, Grohmann & Sprott, 2005](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0148296304002000)).

Music can change how things feel to the touch. In four studies, music that sounded soft made fabric products feel softer, and shoppers were willing to pay more for them. The effect needed the right conditions: the product had to be soft enough for the difference to be felt, and shoppers had to be unaware of the music's influence ([Imschloss & Kuehnl, 2019](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jretai.2019.10.004)).

A scent can hold a memory. When pencils carried an unusual scent, people forgot far less about the brand two weeks later than people given unscented pencils. The lab behind the study reported a drop of 8% in recalled information, against 73% for the unscented group ([Krishna, Lwin & Morrin, 2010](https://doi.org/10.1086/649909); figures as reported in [HBR, 2015](https://hbr.org/2015/03/the-science-of-sensory-marketing)).

Light changes behaviour, not always sales. In a wine shop, brighter lighting led shoppers to examine and handle more bottles. Sales did not change ([Areni & Kim, 1994](https://ro.uow.edu.au/gsbpapers/460)).

Warmth makes people follow the crowd. In warmer rooms, people relied more on other people's choices when picking products and making bets. At a racetrack, bets gathered more around the favourite on warm days ([Huang et al., 2014](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jcps.2013.09.009)).

Sound and scent together reached the street. In Seoul, Dunkin' Donuts released a coffee aroma on city buses whenever its jingle played. HBR reports that visits to outlets near the bus stops rose by 16% and sales by 29% ([HBR, 2015](https://hbr.org/2015/03/the-science-of-sensory-marketing)). This is a campaign result, not a controlled study.

structuredContent.value: Where it stops working

This field has had its warnings. One of its most quoted findings said that brief physical warmth, such as holding a warm cup, made people warmer towards others ([Williams & Bargh, 2008](https://doi.org/10.1126/science.1162548)). Larger repeat studies with more than 1,000 participants in total found no such effect ([Lynott et al., 2014](https://doi.org/10.1027/1864-9335/a000187); [Chabris et al., 2019](https://doi.org/10.1027/1864-9335/a000361)). The lesson is not that the senses do not matter. It is that single, surprising lab results deserve caution until they are repeated.

The store studies above are on firmer ground, but most of them are single studies, in one place, with one or two senses at a time. A major review of store atmospherics concluded that how the full multisensory environment shapes behaviour is still an open question ([Spence et al., 2014](https://doi.org/10.1002/mar.20709)).

And more is not better. Stacking strong cues does not add up to a strong experience. Abercrombie & Fitch combined dark rooms, loud music and heavy fragrance, and many shoppers described the result as overload (see our article on music as a filter).
What this means for hotels, restaurants and bars

Choose the energy first, then set every cue to it. Decide whether a space at a given hour should feel calm, relaxed or lively. Then check light, music, scent and temperature against that one word. A breakfast room can be bright, fresh and lightly paced. The same room at dinner can be dimmer, warmer and slower.

Change the cues together. In Greece, the light on a terrace changes by itself as the sun goes down. If the music still sounds like four in the afternoon at nine in the evening, the cues have drifted apart. Let the music and the lighting follow the sun, not only the clock.

Give the senses one owner. In most venues, light belongs to the architect, scent to a supplier, music to the manager and temperature to maintenance. Someone needs to look at all four together, at least once a season.

Let one sense lead. Brands that do this well usually pick one signature sense and let the others support it. For many hospitality venues that lead is sound, because it fills every corner of the room and changes easily through the day.

When in doubt, simplify. The Christmas study is a useful warning for the coming season. Festive music with no other festive cue, or a festive scent with ordinary music, can make a space feel less coherent than no theme at all. Use the whole theme, or a lighter touch of one cue.
The SensEar checklist: one impression, every sense

items: Do a sensory walk at three times of day. In each space, note the light, the sound, the scent and the temperature. Ask whether they give one consistent impression.
Write one energy word for each space and hour: calm, relaxed or lively. Set every cue to that word.
Fix comfort before atmosphere. A room that is too hot, too cold or too loud cancels every other effort.
Move cues together. When the lights dim, the music should shift in the same quarter of an hour.
Pick a lead sense and let the others support it. Do not let two strong cues compete.
Use seasonal themes completely or lightly. Music, scent and decoration together, or one gentle cue on its own.
Ask your staff. They spend the whole day in the space and notice clashes long before guests mention them.

articles.title: Music licensing for venues in Greece: what you need to know
articles.desc: Why a Spotify account is not enough, which organisations license music for businesses in Greece, and what to check before you press play.
articles.author: SensEar Team
articles.alt: Black-and-white photo of a man playing the guitar for a woman at a taverna table

structuredContent.value: Quick take

When a hotel, restaurant, bar or shop plays music for guests, the law treats it as a public performance. That is true whether the music comes from a streaming app, the radio, a TV or a USB stick. In Greece, a venue that plays commercial music usually needs licences from two kinds of organisations: one for the people who wrote the songs, and one for the people who recorded them ([Law 2121/1993](https://www.lawspot.gr/nomothesia/nomos-2121-1993/); [kstlaw.gr, updated 2026](https://kstlaw.gr/%CE%BF%CF%81%CE%B3%CE%B1%CE%BD%CE%B9%CF%83%CE%BC%CE%BF%CE%AF-%CF%83%CF%85%CE%BB%CE%BB%CE%BF%CE%B3%CE%B9%CE%BA%CE%AE%CF%82-%CE%B4%CE%B9%CE%B1%CF%87%CE%B5%CE%AF%CF%81%CE%B9%CF%83%CE%B7%CF%82/)).
This guide explains who collects what, how fees are set, when music outside these organisations is a real option, and the mistakes we see most often. It is general information, not legal advice.
Why a Spotify account is not enough

A personal streaming subscription gives you the right to listen in private. It does not give you the right to play music to customers. Spotify says so directly: the service is only for personal, non-commercial use, and it cannot be played publicly in bars, restaurants, shops or similar businesses ([Spotify Support](https://support.spotify.com/me-en/article/spotify-public-commercial-use)). The same logic applies to other personal streaming accounts, to YouTube and to your own music files.

Radio and TV are not a way around this. The Hellenic Copyright Organisation (ΟΠΙ) has said that a shop with a radio or TV installation is presumed to use protected music and needs a licence, even if the TV only shows sport ([Lawspot, reporting ΟΠΙ](https://www.lawspot.gr/nomika-nea/nomimi-hrisi-moysikis-se-katastimata-dieykriniseis-apo-ton-organismo-pneymatikis/)).
Who collects what
Every recorded song carries two layers of rights.

The first layer is the song itself: the music and the lyrics. These are authors' rights, and they belong to composers, lyricists and their publishers. In Greece, two licensed organisations collect for them: ΕΔΕΜ and Αυτοδιαχείριση. Each represents its own members and repertoire, so a venue that plays music from both repertoires needs a licence from both.

The second layer is the recording: the singers, the musicians and the record producers. These are called related rights. In Greece they are collected jointly by GEA, which three organisations set up in 2011 so that venues deal with one body instead of three: Grammo for producers, Ερατώ for singers and Απόλλων for musicians ([Ερατώ](https://www.eratospe.org/node/24)).

items: The song (music and lyrics): the rights belong to composers, lyricists and publishers, and venues in Greece get their licence from ΕΔΕΜ and Αυτοδιαχείριση.
The recording: the rights belong to singers, musicians and record producers, and venues in Greece get their licence from GEA (for Grammo, Ερατώ and Απόλλων).

structuredContent.value: Paying one does not settle the other. A venue that plays recorded commercial music normally needs both layers covered.

A short history explains why there are two authors' organisations. For decades, almost all songwriters in Greece were represented by ΑΕΠΙ. In May 2018 the Ministry of Culture permanently revoked ΑΕΠΙ's licence ([iefimerida, 2018](https://www.iefimerida.gr/news/416536/ypoyrgeio-politismoy-kleinei-oristika-tin-aepi)). ΕΔΕΜ was then licensed and started operating in 2020, and today represents about 4,500 rightsholders ([ΕΔΕΜ](https://www.edemrights.gr/el/poioi-eimaste/)). Αυτοδιαχείριση challenged ΕΔΕΜ's licence, and the Council of State rejected the challenge in 2021 ([Powergame, 2021](https://www.powergame.gr/ellada/163746/ste-kalos-anelave-i-edem-ti-diacheirisi-pnevmatikon-dikaiomaton/)).

Only organisations licensed by the Ministry of Culture can collect in Greece. In September 2025 ΟΠΙ reminded businesses that bodies without that licence, including collecting societies based in other EU countries, cannot issue licences for music in Greek restaurants, cafés and shops ([Αυτοδιαχείριση, 2025](https://www.autodia.gr/article/538/mono-foreis-me-adeia-toy-ypoyrgeioy-politismoy-mporoyn-na-syllegoyn-pneymatika-kai-syggenika-dikaiomata)). The full list of licensed organisations is published by ΟΠΙ.
How the fee is set

Each organisation publishes a tariff. It is usually based on the type of business, the size of the space and how central music is to what the venue offers. A beach bar where music is part of the product sits in a different band from a pharmacy with quiet background music.

The tariff is a starting point. Lawyers who work in this area point out that Greek law expects organisations to negotiate with users, and courts have placed businesses in lower bands where music was not essential to them ([kstlaw.gr](https://kstlaw.gr/%CE%BF%CF%81%CE%B3%CE%B1%CE%BD%CE%B9%CF%83%CE%BC%CE%BF%CE%AF-%CF%83%CF%85%CE%BB%CE%BB%CE%BF%CE%B3%CE%B9%CE%BA%CE%AE%CF%82-%CE%B4%CE%B9%CE%B1%CF%87%CE%B5%CE%AF%CF%81%CE%B9%CF%83%CE%B7%CF%82/)). Describe your venue accurately: size, hours, season, and whether music is a background or a reason people come.
Music outside the organisations' repertoire

A venue does not have to use music that the organisations represent. Some suppliers offer music whose creators have not assigned their rights to any Greek organisation. If a venue plays only that music, it does not owe fees to the organisations for it. A Greek police circular from 2015, as reported in 2025, says the same ([Rib and Sea, 2025](https://www.ribandsea.com/news/5315-elegxoi-apo-tin-elliniki-astynomia-sxetika-me-ta-dikaiomata-mousikis-stis-epixeiriseis.html)).
There are three conditions that venues often miss.
First, it must be all of the music, all of the time. One radio station, one TV channel or one staff playlist brings protected music back into the room.

Second, the burden of proof is on the venue. ΟΠΙ has warned that a certificate from a supplier is not enough on its own, and that owners should check carefully what they are buying. The law presumes that a licensed organisation represents the repertoire it declares. That presumption can be challenged, and in one 2022 case a retail chain did so successfully, but only with detailed evidence about where every track came from ([Chambers, 2022](https://chambers.com/articles/greek-collecting-societies-are-not-entitled-to-collect-equitable-remuneration)).

Third, the music has to suit your venue. A legal playlist that does not fit your space costs you in the ways our other articles describe. Some suppliers now also offer music generated entirely by AI and say that no fees apply to it. As far as we can find, no Greek court has ruled on this yet.
Mistakes we see often

items: Thinking the municipal permit covers it. The permission to use music that a business declares to the municipality is a separate matter from copyright. One does not replace the other.
Forgetting the TV. A screen showing a match with the sound on counts, and so does a radio in the kitchen that guests can hear.

Hotel rooms. Under EU case law, TVs and radios in hotel rooms can count as communication to the public ([CJEU, SGAE v Rafael Hoteles, C-306/05](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX:62005CJ0306)).
Live music and DJs. A band playing other people's songs still uses the songwriters' rights. A DJ playing recordings uses both layers.
Seasonal venues. If you open from May to October, say so when you apply. The season affects the fee.
Paying the wrong body. Check that the organisation is licensed in Greece before you pay anyone.

structuredContent.value: What happens if a venue has no licence

The organisations can claim the fee through the courts. Under Article 65 of Law 2121/1993, compensation for unlicensed use is normally at least double the fee that would have been paid. Article 66 also provides for criminal penalties, including prison terms and fines from €2,900 upwards, and it was amended again in 2025 ([kstlaw.gr](https://kstlaw.gr/%CE%BF%CF%81%CE%B3%CE%B1%CE%BD%CE%B9%CF%83%CE%BC%CE%BF%CE%AF-%CF%83%CF%85%CE%BB%CE%BB%CE%BF%CE%B3%CE%B9%CE%BA%CE%AE%CF%82-%CE%B4%CE%B9%CE%B1%CF%87%CE%B5%CE%AF%CF%81%CE%B9%CF%83%CE%B7%CF%82/); [Lawspot, Article 66](https://www.lawspot.gr/nomothesia/n-2121-1993/arthro-66-nomos-2121-1993-poinikes-kyroseis/)). In 2025, local reports described police checks in businesses across the country ([Rib and Sea, 2025](https://www.ribandsea.com/news/5315-elegxoi-apo-tin-elliniki-astynomia-sxetika-me-ta-dikaiomata-mousikis-stis-epixeiriseis.html)).
The collecting organisations themselves cannot impose fines. They can ask for payment and go to court.
The SensEar checklist: before you press play

items: List every source of sound guests can hear: speakers, TVs, radios, live music, DJs, staff phones.
Decide your route: licensed commercial music, music outside the organisations' repertoire, or a mix by space.
If you play commercial music, cover both layers: the songs (ΕΔΕΜ and Αυτοδιαχείριση, depending on repertoire) and the recordings (GEA).
Describe your venue accurately when you apply: size, opening months, hours and the role music plays.
If you choose music outside the repertoire, get written terms from the supplier and keep records of what you play. Remove every other source.
Check the organisation is on ΟΠΙ's list before you pay.
Keep licences and receipts where staff can find them during a check.
Review it every year. Repertoires, tariffs and rules change.

articles.title: When less is more: sound fatigue and the role of silence
articles.desc: Noise is diners' top complaint, and too much sound costs venues money. What research says about volume, constant music and quiet, and how to plan less sound into the day.
articles.author: SensEar Team
articles.alt: Woman seen from behind, sitting alone at a table by the sea with a cocktail

structuredContent.value: Quick take

For most venues, the problem is not too little music. It is too much: too loud, too constant, too many sources at once. Noise is the complaint diners mention most, ahead of service and prices. A lab study found that people's willingness to spend time and money starts to fall at background levels that many busy restaurants pass early in the evening.
This article is not a case against music. Guests generally prefer the right music to none. It is a case for planning sound the way you plan light: with levels, pauses and the occasional dark corner.
A generation that turns the music down

In 2025, the magazine Dazed spoke to young people who had stopped listening to music altogether. One of them said she had realised she spent more time skipping songs, looking for the "right" one, than listening. Another described the change as a fog lifting. The writer's conclusion was that they were not rejecting music. They were rejecting music as constant background noise, something to fill every gap rather than something to listen to ([Dazed, 2025](https://www.dazeddigital.com/music/article/66709/1/young-people-are-turning-their-backs-on-music)).

This is a small trend, not a mass movement. The same article quotes a 2024 survey of 2,100 young people in the UK, in which 71% said music is a big part of who they are. But it says something useful to anyone who runs a venue. Many guests arrive with ears that have been full all day. A room that offers a little less, chosen with care, can feel like a relief rather than an absence.
What the research found

items: Noise is the top complaint. In Zagat's 2018 survey of about 13,000 American diners, noise ranked as the most irritating part of eating out, ahead of service and prices ([White Hutchinson, 2018](https://whitehutchinson.com/news/lenews/2018/january/article103.shtml)).

Willingness to spend falls early. In a lab study, 28 people read aloud over recorded restaurant noise at levels from 35 to 85 dB(A). They started to feel disturbed above about 52 dB(A), and their willingness to spend time and money in that restaurant started to fall at about the same point. Above about 57 dB(A), the effort they put into their voice rose twice as fast. The researcher's advice was to keep background noise below 50 to 55 dB(A) ([Bottalico, 2018](https://acoustics.org/4ans11-lombard-effect-in-restaurant-setting-how-much-would-you-spend-to-eat-at-this-restaurant-pasquale-bottalico/)).

Real rooms are louder than that. Recordings from 15 restaurants, cafés and bars in Singapore ranged from about 61 to 76 dB(A). In cafés, louder recordings were rated less pleasant. In bars, louder recordings were rated more pleasant ([Lindborg & Friberg, 2016](https://doi.org/10.3390/app6120405)). The right level depends on what the room is for.

The wrong music can be worse than none. In a 20-week study in 16 Swedish restaurants, random chart hits that did not fit the brand performed below the weeks with no music at all, according to the study report ([Soundtrack Your Brand & HUI Research, 2017](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/315800050_The_impact_of_music_in_restaurants)). Our earlier post on brand-fit music covers the same study from the other side.

Quiet hours are now routine in some shops. Morrisons runs a weekly quieter hour in its UK stores: music off, lights lowered, no announcements, quieter checkouts ([The Scotsman](https://www.scotsman.com/business/supermarket-to-introduce-quieter-hour-in-all-of-its-stores-583881)). Tesco trialled the same idea after a parent of an autistic child described the problem as sensory overload ([The Grocer](https://www.thegrocer.co.uk/news/tesco-trials-quiet-hour-to-help-autistic-shoppers/547463.article)).

Even loud venues are told to offer quiet. The World Health Organization's 2022 standard for safe listening at venues and events recommends a maximum average level, sound monitoring, and quiet zones where people can rest their ears ([WHO, 2022](https://www.who.int/news/item/02-03-2022-who-releases-new-standard-to-tackle-rising-threat-of-hearing-loss)).

structuredContent.value: Where it stops working

Silence is not the goal. Field studies in shops and restaurants usually find that people stay longer and spend more with suitable music than without it (see our post on how music shapes buyer behaviour). A completely silent dining room also has its own problems: every plate, every coffee machine and every conversation at the next table becomes easy to hear. Good background music masks those sounds and gives guests privacy.

The numbers also need care. The 52 dB(A) threshold comes from a small lab study with students reading aloud, presented at a conference, not from a full journal paper. It points in a clear direction, but it is not a rule for every room. And as the Singapore study shows, a lively bar is a different case from a quiet café.
What this means for hotels, restaurants and bars

Turn it down before you turn it off. Many venues fall into a slow spiral. As the room fills, guests talk louder, staff turn the music up so it can still be heard, and guests talk louder again. This is a common pattern, and it has a name in acoustics: the Lombard effect, the habit of raising our voice in noise. The fix is a fixed maximum volume for each part of the day, set when the room is full, not when it is empty.

Use fewer sources at once. Background music, a TV with sport, a radio in the kitchen and a coffee grinder add up. Before you change the playlist, count how many sounds a guest hears at one table, and remove one.

Plan dynamics, not just playlists. A day needs quieter stretches as much as busy ones. Breakfast, the first hour after opening and the slow afternoon can sit noticeably lower than the evening peak. In a hotel, one lounge, library corner or terrace with little or no music gives guests a choice.

Fix the room before buying louder speakers. Hard floors, glass and bare walls make every sound linger. Soft materials, acoustic panels and better placed speakers often let you play the same music at a lower level and still be heard (see our [Audio Upgrades](/services/audio-upgrades/) service).
Watch for repetition. Fatigue is not only about volume. A short playlist that loops several times a day tires regulars and staff long before it tires a first-time guest.
The SensEar checklist: less sound, better sound

items: Measure at the table, at peak time. A free phone app is enough to start. If guests need to raise their voice to talk, the room is too loud for dining.
Set a maximum volume for each part of the day, and set it when the room is full.
Count the sound sources a guest hears at one table. Remove at least one.
Give the day a shape: lower in the morning and the slow afternoon, fuller at the evening peak.
Offer one quiet option: a corner, a terrace, a lounge or a quiet hour.
Treat the acoustics before you raise the volume.
Ask your staff which tracks they are tired of. If they hear a song five times a day, guests who stay for hours will hear it too.

articles.title: Sonic seasoning: how sound changes taste
articles.desc: What 94 studies found about pitch, music, noise and taste, and how restaurants and bars can use it without gimmicks.
articles.author: SensEar Team
articles.alt: Diner in a dark suit with a napkin tucked into his collar, cutting a vinyl record with a knife and fork next to a glass of red wine

structuredContent.value: Quick take

Taste is not made on the tongue alone. The brain builds it from everything that arrives at the same time, and sound is part of that mix. A systematic review of 94 studies found two consistent patterns: people match tastes to sounds in a predictable way (sweet and sour with high notes, bitter with low ones), and the sound in the room can shift how sweet, bitter or strong a dish or drink seems ([Guedes et al., 2023](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.foodqual.2023.104856)).
The effects are real but modest. They do not turn a bad dish into a good one. They do decide whether a good dish is tasted at all.
Why sound reaches the tongue
Two things happen at once.

The first is a mapping. When people are asked to pick a note for a taste, they choose high notes for sweet and sour and low notes for bitter. Piano tends to read as sweet, brass as bitter. The pattern holds across countries and across real products such as beer, chocolate and juice ([Crisinel & Spence, 2010](https://doi.org/10.3758/APP.72.7.1994); [Guedes et al., 2023](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.foodqual.2023.104856)).

The second is emotion. Music a guest likes makes sweetness stand out for longer. Music a guest dislikes brings bitterness forward. In studies with gelato and beer, this emotional route showed up clearly and consistently ([Kantono et al., 2016](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.appet.2016.02.143); [Reinoso Carvalho et al., 2017](https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-319-67738-5_19)).
So a venue works with two levers: what the music suggests, and how the music makes people feel.
What the research found

items: Custom tracks moved the taste of a beer. Belgian beers were rated sweeter with a track composed to sound "sweet" and more alcoholic with a track composed to sound "bitter". Same beer, same glass ([Reinoso Carvalho et al., 2017](https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-319-67738-5_19)).

Liked music means sweeter, disliked music means more bitter. With chocolate gelato, sweetness dominated longer when guests heard music they had chosen themselves, and bitterness dominated when they heard music they disliked ([Kantono et al., 2016](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.appet.2016.02.143)).

Loud noise flattens sweet and salty. Under loud white noise, food was rated less sweet and less salty. In a simulated aircraft cabin, sweetness dropped while umami rose, which is one reason tomato juice tastes better in the air than on the ground ([Woods et al., 2011](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.foodqual.2010.07.003); [Yan & Dando, 2015](https://doi.org/10.1037/xhp0000044)).

The soundscape sets the direction. The same ice cream read sweeter in a café soundscape with forest sounds and more bitter in a café soundscape with machine noise. Bar, fast-food and food-court soundscapes pushed bitterness forward; park and café soundscapes pushed sweetness forward ([Guedes et al., 2023](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.foodqual.2023.104856), Table 7).

Wine is sensitive too. A white wine was rated sweeter with classical music than in silence, and music changed which sensations dominated in a red wine, especially bitterness ([Guedes et al., 2023](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.foodqual.2023.104856), Table 5).

structuredContent.value: Where it stops working
Honest limits matter more than headlines here.

In a real chocolate shop, a custom soundtrack did not change how customers rated a praline compared with the shop's own soundscape. Lab effects do not always survive a busy floor ([Guedes et al., 2023](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.foodqual.2023.104856)).
Noise results are mixed. Some studies found a clear drop in sweetness, others found nothing. The type of noise and the taste in question both matter.

And one guest's "pleasant" is another guest's "annoying". Several authors suggest that shared mappings (high pitch for sweet) work for a room full of people, while emotional effects depend on who is sitting at the table. A venue cannot play each guest their favourite song. It can avoid music that a large part of its guests dislike.
What this means for restaurants, bars and hotels

Chefs have played with this for years. Heston Blumenthal served a seafood dish with headphones playing waves and seagulls. Breweries have released beers with a song attached. Most venues do not need a stunt. They need three things to be in order.

First, the noise floor. If guests have to raise their voice, the sweet and salty notes in the food are already being lost. [Acoustic treatment](/services/audio-upgrades/) and sensible volume are the cheapest flavour upgrade a kitchen will ever get.

Second, the emotional tone. Music the room enjoys makes the food taste sweeter and rounder. Music the room tolerates makes it taste sharper. This is one more reason why "the owner's playlist" is a risk, not a shortcut.

Third, the match. A dessert course, a wine list built around acidity, a bitter-forward cocktail menu: each one has a sound profile that supports it. Lighter, higher, consonant music for sweet and sour; lower, slower, richer music for bitter and umami. Nobody will notice the logic. They will notice that the food tasted the way the menu promised.
The SensEar checklist: sonic seasoning without the gimmicks

items: Measure your noise floor at peak. If conversation needs a raised voice, fix acoustics and volume before you touch the playlist.
Programme by course, not only by hour. Lighter, higher-pitched, consonant music when dessert and wine are on the table; lower and warmer music for the savoury main.
Keep the room on your guests' side. The strongest effect in the research is liking. Review the music with your audience in mind, not the team's taste.
Treat tastings as events. Wine, coffee, chocolate and spirits tastings are where matched sound shows up most. Build a short, matched set for each.
Do not promise magic. Sonic seasoning sharpens what the kitchen already does well. It does not replace it.
Test it. Run two matched weeks, change only the music, and ask guests one question about the dessert or the wine. Keep what moves.

articles.author: SensEar Team

structuredContent.value: Luxury and lifestyle hotels do not leave music to chance
They treat sound as part of the brand system: researched, tested and revised, so that the music shapes mood and memory with the same care as the interior.
Eight examples to learn from
W Hotels

Music is built into the brand, from artist partnerships to purpose-built recording spaces like the W Sound Suite, which hosts [sessions and programming](https://w-hotels.marriott.com/article/behind-the-dj-booth-with-uner/) in select properties.
Soho House

In-house music leads curate evolving playlists that follow the look and feel of each House and its dayparts, and [publish them on the major platforms](https://www.sohohouse.com/house-notes/issue-4/dom-chung-soho-house-playlist) so members can take the sound with them.
The Standard Hotels

For 25 years the group has treated music as part of the stay, and recently archived that approach in ["The Standard Soundtrack"](https://www.standardhotels.com/culture/the-standard-soundtrack), a series that captures the brand's sonic point of view year by year.
Ace Hotel

A long-running music culture shows up in label collaborations, live sessions and branded streams that [carry the property's sound](https://www.cntraveler.com/stories/2015-09-10/ace-hotel-cranks-the-cool-up-to-11-with-vinyl) beyond the lobby.
Rosewood Hotels (Scarfes Bar, London)
Partnered with the specialist agency Music Concierge on venue-specific soundtracks. Scarfes Bar is widely cited for its atmosphere and for the live jazz programme that anchors the bar's identity.
25hours Hotels
Publishes ["25hours Music DNA"](https://open.spotify.com/playlist/2GYyzEKnynSVi5eO2f6eGL), a living playlist identity that keeps the brand's playful personality consistent across properties.
EDITION Hotels
Maintains [branded mixes and sets](https://soundcloud.com/editionhotels) on its official channels, a contemporary point of view that matches the brand's cultural positioning.
Mama Shelter
Regular DJ programming and [public mixtapes](https://www.mixcloud.com/mamashelter/playlists/mama-loves-music/) keep the energy matched to each location while showcasing resident talent.
Two more to watch
Virgin Hotels
Runs ongoing music initiatives and publishes [official playlists](https://virginhotels.com/hearthis/), often tailored to each city and venue.
Moxy Hotels
Uses public [branded playlists](https://moxy-hotels.marriott.com/) to express a youthful, high-energy identity that fits the social lobby concept.
What these groups do differently

items: They treat sound like design.
They programme by daypart and by zone.
They combine human taste with data.
They publish their playlists, so the sound travels beyond the property.

structuredContent.value: Short take: music shapes how guests feel, what they remember and, in the studies below, how they spend
The leading hotel groups treat the stay as one design system: architecture, materials, light and the sound in each room are decided together.
Music and the guest experience
Music is the quickest way to set the mood of a room, and one of the cheapest. The right selection matches what the guest expects from the place and what the place wants to say.

[Slow background music](https://academic.oup.com/jcr/article-abstract/13/2/286/1846377) can lengthen dwell and lift sales in certain contexts, while [faster tempos](https://www.deepdyve.com/lp/sage/using-background-music-to-affect-the-behavior-of-supermarket-shoppers-0MSfbyjTU0) speed up the pace when turnover is the priority. Music can also alter [perceived time](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S014829639900003X) and how people judge the environment and what it sells, which is useful for [managing service flow](https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/pdf/10.1177/00222437221150930) and guest satisfaction.
Music and brand identity

Sound is part of brand memory. Consistent musical choices make a space feel on-brand and recognisable, the same way colour, typography and materials do. [Research in marketing and consumer psychology](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0001691824002105) shows that sonic branding and music cues can shape recall, perceived fit and purchase intent. Playlists aligned with the space and the feel the brand intends give it [an edge](https://etheses.whiterose.ac.uk/id/eprint/22404/1/Wong%202018%20-%20Sound%20Branding%20-%20FINAL%20DEC%202018.pdf) that generic background music does not.
Music and the staff

Music also affects the people who work in the room. [Reviews and practitioner summaries](https://hbr.org/2022/09/can-music-make-you-more-productive) suggest that background music can help mood regulation and short-term performance on certain tasks, which is why clear rules about what plays when, curated by daypart, matter. [An industry survey](https://cloudcovermusic.com/research/music-at-work-research) points the same way, with large shares of employees reporting they work better with appropriate music in the background.

Music belongs next to visual and scent design in hospitality. [Studies in retail and restaurants](https://academic.oup.com/jcr/article-abstract/13/2/286/1846377) show that tempo and style change pace, perceived time and spend; the same mechanisms apply in a hotel when the music is chosen for each room and hour. [Sonic identity](/services/sonic-identity/) is that decision taken at brand level.

articles.title: How brand-fit music converts browsers into buyers
articles.desc: What the retail research found about brand-fit music, and what it means for bars, hotels and shops.
articles.alt: Restaurant ambiance demonstrating music's impact on customer sales and behavior
articles.author: SensEar Team

structuredContent.value: Sound reaches people before the menu does, and retail uses it least

Walk into any bar, hotel or restaurant and you feel the space before you read a line of the menu: lighting, materials, layout. Sound is part of that first impression too, quietly steering attention, pace and preference; [Bitner's servicescape framework](https://www.jstor.org/stable/1252042) treats music as one of the core ambient cues.
The evidence for brand-fit music

Large-scale [field research](https://ideas.repec.org/p/hhs/huiwps/0121.html) moved this question from hunch to numbers. In a multi-month experiment across 16 high-traffic [restaurants](/industries/music-for-restaurants-and-bars/), playlists that matched the brand's personality outperformed random chart hits, with [revenues about 9.1% higher](https://ideas.repec.org/p/hhs/huiwps/0121.html).

Earlier work had already shown that music changes shopper behaviour: [slow-tempo music](https://music2biz.com/wp-content/uploads/2017/04/Using-Background-Music-to-Affect-the-Behavior-of-Supermarket-Shoppers.pdf) reduced walking speed and increased supermarket sales. And music that matches the context can tilt what people choose: in a [wine-aisle study](https://archive.org/download/wikipedia-scholarly-sources-corpus/10.1037%252F0002-9432.71.2.245.zip/10.1037%252F0021-9010.84.2.271.pdf), French and German wine sales swung with the nationality of the music.
What brand-fit actually means

[Brand-fit music](/services/signature-playlists/) works like your interior palette, for the ears: it reflects the brand's values, tone and intended pace, so the sound is unmistakably yours. Customer-fit music, playing only what you think guests prefer, often dissolves into a beige mix that blurs the place, especially with a varied audience.
Why it works: the senses do not operate alone

Sound crosses over into taste, time perception and arousal. Reviews in multisensory perception show that sonic cues can reshape [flavour experience](https://ora.ox.ac.uk/objects/uuid%3Af7af7995-1ba5-4557-bdb1-782dd9185583/download_file?safe_filename=Spence-et-al-2021-Commercializing-sonic-seasoning.pdf&type_of_work=Journal+article) ("sonic seasoning") and the hospitality moment as a whole. This sits inside [servicescape theory](https://academic.oup.com/jcr/article-abstract/13/2/286/1846377), where ambient conditions (music, scent, temperature) shape both customer and staff outcomes.
What the data says in plain numbers
Brand-fit playlists beat random popular tracks, with a [sales lift of about 9.1%](https://ideas.repec.org/p/hhs/huiwps/0121.html) in a real restaurant chain.
Mixing recognisable and lesser-known tracks, as long as both fit the brand, improves results further: it avoids listener fatigue while keeping the identity.

Tempo and congruence matter: [slower music](https://music2biz.com/wp-content/uploads/2017/04/Using-Background-Music-to-Affect-the-Behavior-of-Supermarket-Shoppers.pdf) can increase dwell and basket size, and culturally congruent music can nudge [category choice](https://archive.org/download/wikipedia-scholarly-sources-corpus/10.1037%252F0002-9432.71.2.245.zip/10.1037%252F0021-9010.84.2.271.pdf).
Where to start

If you run a [bar or restaurant](/industries/music-for-restaurants-and-bars/) or a [hotel](/industries/music-for-hotels-and-resorts/) and the music was never really chosen, [tell us about the room](/contact/).

articles.title: What exactly does a music curator do?
articles.desc: What a music curator does: listening, brand and space diagnostics, building the programme, and keeping it current.
articles.alt: Professional music curator selecting tracks for bespoke venue playlists
articles.author: SensEar Team

structuredContent.value: A music curator decides what a place sounds like

They build playlists and ambient programmes for a space, chosen so that the music fits the room, the hour and the brand. Unlike DJs, who perform live and read a crowd in the moment, [curators work upstream](https://thearf-org-unified-admin.s3.amazonaws.com/ARF%20Councils/ARF_Creative_SonicBranding_2024_10.pdf): they turn the brief, the context and what is known about listening into a programme a venue can run every day, in retail, hospitality, offices, events and installations.
Four parts of the job
1. Listening, all the time

Curators follow new releases and catalogue gems across genres, regions and moods. The goal is not "good music" but fit: tracks whose tempo, timbre, energy and familiarity match the [experience the space is meant to produce](https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/psychology/articles/10.3389/fpsyg.2023.1236006/full).

Under the craft sits neuroscience: [peak emotional responses](https://www.brainmusic.org/MBB91%20Webpage/Blood_Zatorre_2001.pdf) to music recruit the brain's reward circuitry (ventral striatum, amygdala, orbitofrontal cortex), which is why the right track at the right moment can change how a room feels.
2. Brand and space diagnostics

Before a single track is placed, the curator reads the context: vision, clientele, dayparts, acoustic constraints and the behaviour the space needs (linger, browse, buy, relax, talk). The brief may include [speech privacy](https://cambridgesound.com/sound-masking-references/) or confidentiality needs; in those cases curators work alongside [acoustic design](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2405844024130733) and [sound masking](https://cambridgesound.com/sound-masking-references/) so that conversations stay private while the room stays comfortable.
3. Playlist systems, not templates
From a blank canvas, curators design playlists that express the venue's identity across the day: opening calm, midday energy, golden-hour warmth, late-night minimalism. The mix balances:

items: [Familiar versus new](https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/psychology/articles/10.3389/fpsyg.2023.1236006/full), to balance comfort with discovery.

[Tempo](https://music2biz.com/wp-content/uploads/2017/04/Using-Background-Music-to-Affect-the-Behavior-of-Supermarket-Shoppers.pdf), to influence pace and dwell time; a [lever](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0969698912000732) repeatedly shown to shift [shopping](https://academic.oup.com/jcr/article-abstract/13/2/286/1846377) and [dining behaviour](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0950329324000971).
Vocal versus instrumental, to manage cognitive load and conversation.
Representation and fairness in [artist selection](https://dl.acm.org/doi/fullHtml/10.1145/3640457.3688163), away from the known biases of recommender systems.

structuredContent.value: Brand personality counts too. Sonic logos and short audio signatures, for example, can strengthen perceived sincerity or ruggedness when their [musical features](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0148296323005283) match the brand's traits.
4. Keeping it current

Curation is not "set and forget". A programme stays alive with scheduled rotation, seasonal changes, adjustments for busy periods and feedback from the floor; tired tracks come out, new material goes in. Sonic branding programmes likewise [measure memory](https://thearf-org-unified-admin.s3.amazonaws.com/ARF%20Councils/ARF_Creative_SonicBranding_2024_10.pdf), recognition and emotional response, and revise their assets over time.
Why it works: the evidence

Tempo steers pace and spend. [Slow-tempo music](https://music2biz.com/wp-content/uploads/2017/04/Using-Background-Music-to-Affect-the-Behavior-of-Supermarket-Shoppers.pdf) can lengthen time in store and increase sales; similar effects appear in [restaurants](https://academic.oup.com/jcr/article-abstract/13/2/286/1846377), where slower music extends [dining duration](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0950329324000971).

Emotion is the engine. Peak musical pleasure lights up the [brain's reward network](https://www.brainmusic.org/MBB91%20Webpage/Blood_Zatorre_2001.pdf), which is why a well-chosen programme can shift mood and memory.

From jingles to systems. Sonic branding is now measured like visual identity: [assets are tested](https://thearf-org-unified-admin.s3.amazonaws.com/ARF%20Councils/ARF_Creative_SonicBranding_2024_10.pdf), revised and governed for [recall and fit](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0148296323005283).

Privacy matters in real rooms. [Sound masking](https://cambridgesound.com/sound-masking-references/) and [spatial design](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2405844024130733) improve speech privacy without killing the ambience, which matters in healthcare, offices and [premium retail](https://cambridgesound.com/sound-masking-references/).
Curators and DJs

DJs perform; curators prepare. A curator builds a programme a team can run every day, across zones and locations, grounded in the brand, in how people hear a room, and in [measurement](https://thearf-org-unified-admin.s3.amazonaws.com/ARF%20Councils/ARF_Creative_SonicBranding_2024_10.pdf).
What this looks like as a service

That is the work: [daily playlists](/services/signature-playlists/), [sonic identity](/services/sonic-identity/) and the [acoustics](/services/audio-upgrades/) they play through. [Hear the work in place](/case-studies/).

articles.title: The music curation cycle
articles.desc: Why music curation is a continuing loop rather than a one-off delivery, and what changes after launch.
articles.alt: Music analytics and optimization process for venue soundscapes
articles.author: SensEar Team

structuredContent.value: Music is more than ambience

The right track at the right moment reshapes how a room feels. In a lobby, calm mid-tempo selections [ease arrivals and reduce noise fatigue](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0969698923002345). In a dining room, steady rhythmic music [supports conversation and the pacing of service](https://academic.oup.com/jcr/article-abstract/13/2/286/1846377). Late in the evening, [more energy and tempo](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/pdf/10.1080/1750984X.2011.631026) keep guests engaged for longer.
At SensEar, those shifts are designed on purpose, one zone and one hour at a time.
Curation is a loop, not a checkbox

Good programming is never "set it and forget it". It starts with a launch and continues through listening and refinement: tracks that feel tired or get skipped come out, new material that fits the audience goes in. The research gives the direction: [slower music](https://music2biz.com/wp-content/uploads/2017/04/Using-Background-Music-to-Affect-the-Behavior-of-Supermarket-Shoppers.pdf) can increase time on site and spending in certain contexts, and in restaurants [slower tempos](https://academic.oup.com/jcr/article-abstract/13/2/286/1846377) have been linked with guests staying longer and ordering more, while faster tempos help turn tables when needed.
Humans in the mix

Our curators are musicians, DJs and musicologists with backgrounds in hospitality venues, music production, radio and technology. They spend time in your space to understand the flow of service and the rhythm of the day. The programme is then tested where it will play, because the research is specific to each setting: tempo curves for [classes in a fitness studio](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1469029224000554), energy arcs for a [full dinner service](https://academic.oup.com/jcr/article-abstract/13/2/286/1846377), quiet sets that [avoid listener fatigue](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/pdf/10.1080/1750984X.2011.631026) in a spa.
Staying current

What works today can feel dated in a few months; culture moves and tastes shift. Context steers choices too: when background music matches a cultural cue, guests are more likely to choose the congruent product, as in the retail test where [French music increased French wine sales](https://archive.org/download/wikipedia-scholarly-sources-corpus/10.1037%252F0002-9432.71.2.245.zip/10.1037%252F0021-9010.84.2.271.pdf). Programming benefits from following trends and audience response rather than relying on a static algorithm.
The craft and the science

Every set is shaped by feel and by data: tempo, intensity, cadence and BPM, matched to the arc of the room. Music also changes how time is perceived; retail experiments show it can alter [both perceived and actual shopping duration](https://rybn.org/ANTI/ADMXI/documentation/ALGORITHM_DOCUMENTATION/HARMONY_OF_THE_SPEARS/BACKGROUND_MUSIC_STUDIES/EFFECT_ON_CONSUMPTION/2000_The_Effects_of_Music_in_a_Retail_Setting_on_Real_and_Perceived_Shopping_Times.pdf), which affects evaluations and spend.

Fitness studios: plan build-ups, peaks and recovery. [Faster tempos](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1469029224000554) align better as intensity rises and can [improve affect and perceived exertion](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/pdf/10.1080/1750984X.2011.631026).
Restaurants and bars: [slower tempos](https://academic.oup.com/jcr/article-abstract/13/2/286/1846377) to lengthen stays when wanted, a faster pace to support quicker turns at rush hour.
Spas and lounges: gentle entries, stable middles and [unhurried fades](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/pdf/10.1080/1750984X.2011.631026) keep the calm without dulling the room.

Retail and galleries: align the cues. When [scent and music arousal levels match](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0022435901000422), shopper evaluations improve, which argues for tuning the whole atmosphere, not just the playlist. A [public preprint](https://www.researchgate.net/profile/Jochen-Wirtz/publication/222542870_Congruency_of_Scent_and_Music_as_a_Driver_of_In-Store_Evaluations_and_Behavior/links/59f47c0a458515547c21c2be/Congruency-of-Scent-and-Music-as-a-Driver-of-In-Store-Evaluations-and-Behavior.pdf) of the study is also available.
What you get with SensEar

items: Programming that evolves with your clientele and dayparts
Curators who listen inside your real service flow
Regular updates that keep sets fresh
Taste and data together, instead of one-size-fits-all music

articles.title: Building a brand people can hear
articles.desc: A six-step framework for deciding how a brand should sound, and which touchpoints to start with.
articles.alt: Brand materials laid out beside reference playlists
articles.author: SensEar Team

structuredContent.value: Why sound is your most underrated brand asset

Brand identity is more than visuals. It is the whole set of signals that help people recognise you and trust what you deliver: name, logo, typography, colour, packaging, physical spaces. In a crowded market, consistent sound cues cut through quickly, travel far and stay in memory. [Sensory marketing research](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1057740811000830) shows that engaging several senses strengthens perception, judgement and behaviour, and sound is unusually efficient at doing this at scale.
What a brand really is

A brand is a promise people can identify instantly and rely on consistently. Customers use brand cues to infer quality before they buy. Visual consistency matters, and colour is often said to lift recognition by 80 percent, though [that statistic is frequently misquoted](https://reviewinc.com/2024/08/14/color-increases-brand-recognition/) and context-dependent: it originally concerned [document processing, not logos](https://www.insights4print.ceo/2019/02/color-increases-brand-recognition-by-80-the-real-contents-of-the-loyola-study-revealed/).
The power of sonic branding

Music and sound are immediate, emotional and memorable. Field experiments show that background music can shape traffic and lift sales, especially when tempo and mode are chosen for the context rather than at random. [Research in a supermarket](https://music2biz.com/wp-content/uploads/2017/04/Using-Background-Music-to-Affect-the-Behavior-of-Supermarket-Shoppers.pdf) found that slow-tempo music lengthened shopping time and increased sales compared with fast-tempo tracks, and [tempo and mode interact](https://www.researchgate.net/profile/Klemens-Knoeferle/publication/227451750_It_is_all_in_the_mix_The_interactive_effect_of_music_tempo_and_mode_on_in-store_sales/links/0a85e530360b6bd8a7000000/It-is-all-in-the-mix-The-interactive-effect-of-music-tempo-and-mode-on-in-store-sales.pdf) in their effect on in-store sales, so a playlist should be composed with both in mind.

Congruence matters. When the music fits the offer, people choose in line with it: in a [classic wine-aisle study](https://archive.org/download/wikipedia-scholarly-sources-corpus/10.1037%252F0002-9432.71.2.245.zip/10.1037%252F0021-9010.84.2.271.pdf), French music increased French wine sales and German music increased German wine sales, without a single spoken word.

Sonic logos add a short, distinctive audio signature that supports recall and recognition. [Recent research](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0148296323005283) links well-designed sonic logos to stronger memory and to brand-personality fit, including traits like sincerity or ruggedness when the musical features match the brand.
A six-step framework for deciding how a brand should sound
Use these six steps to align sound with the brand promise.

items: 1. Identify your priority customers and what moves them: use interviews and journey mapping to find where sound can reduce friction or heighten emotion, and anchor the findings in [sensory marketing principles](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1057740811000830) so you design for perception and behaviour, not just taste in music.

2. Define a value proposition people can hear: translate it into sonic territories. Calm expertise suggests slower tempos and stable modes; energetic discovery suggests higher tempos and bright timbres. [Tempo and mode](https://www.researchgate.net/profile/Klemens-Knoeferle/publication/227451750_It_is_all_in_the_mix_The_interactive_effect_of_music_tempo_and_mode_on_in-store_sales/links/0a85e530360b6bd8a7000000/It-is-all-in-the-mix-The-interactive-effect-of-music-tempo-and-mode-on-in-store-sales.pdf) influence pace and purchase behaviour, so plan with both.

3. Assess competitor soundscapes: audit their playlists, voice and any sound logos. [Sonic branding is still under-researched](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/pdf/10.1080/02650487.2023.2273075) relative to its impact, which leaves room to differentiate with evidence-led craft rather than copycat playlists.

4. Design the core sonic assets: a modular system of a primary sonic logo, short stingers, UX sounds and environment-specific playlists, with [musical features that match the brand personality](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0148296323005283) so the audio signals the same traits as the visuals.

5. Make the promise testable: say how sound supports it, for example a calmer check-in with low-arousal tracks in lobbies and rooms, and test it against dwell time, service ratings and repeat-visit intent. [Supermarket studies](https://music2biz.com/wp-content/uploads/2017/04/Using-Background-Music-to-Affect-the-Behavior-of-Supermarket-Shoppers.pdf) show that music can measurably change pace and purchases, so treat playlists as something to measure, not as filler.

6. Activate the right touchpoints: prioritise where customers can hear the promise. In hospitality and retail that means entrances, lobbies, dining areas, fitting rooms, apps, phone systems and short-form video. Make congruence the rule: the [wine-aisle study](https://archive.org/download/wikipedia-scholarly-sources-corpus/10.1037%252F0002-9432.71.2.245.zip/10.1037%252F0021-9010.84.2.271.pdf) shows how aligning music with context quietly tilts choice.

structuredContent.value: Why sound is worth the effort first

Sound works instantly, sets the emotional temperature and is easy to standardise across locations and channels. Integrated into the brand system, music and a sonic logo become the voice of the brand that customers recognise before they look up. For hospitality brands that means consistent quality cues, supported by a growing body of work in [sensory marketing](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1057740811000830) and [sonic branding research](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/pdf/10.1080/02650487.2023.2273075).
Where this becomes a service
If you want a musical direction your teams and agencies can follow without you in the room, that is [sonic identity design](/services/sonic-identity/). [Hear the work in place](/case-studies/).
