articles.title: How music shapes buyer behaviour
articles.desc: What field studies in real shops and restaurants measured about music, pace and spending, and where the effects held.
articles.alt: Retail environment showing background music influence on shopping behavior
articles.author: SensEar Team

structuredContent.value: Quick take

Music can make people stay longer and spend more, but the result depends on who is in the room and what kind of place you run. A [field study with real shoppers](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0969698912000732) found clear lifts in time and spending on music days, with different patterns by gender and by type of store.

Research in restaurants and supermarkets finds similar effects tied to tempo and song choice: the [classic restaurant tempo study](https://www.jstor.org/stable/2489234) and the [supermarket pacing study](https://music2biz.com/wp-content/uploads/2017/04/Using-Background-Music-to-Affect-the-Behavior-of-Supermarket-Shoppers.pdf).
Why sound changes behaviour

The cues in a store or venue shape feelings like pleasure and alertness, and those feelings lead people to approach or avoid: to explore, talk to staff, buy, or leave. Environmental psychology describes this path in the [PAD model](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0022435997900166).
What the field data found

items: More time and more spend with music. In real stores, [shoppers stayed longer and spent more](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0969698912000732) when music played than when the store was quiet.

Tempo steers pace. Slower tracks tend to slow movement and can lift basket size or drink orders, while faster tracks speed things up when you need quicker turns, [in restaurants](https://www.jstor.org/stable/2489234) as [in supermarkets](https://music2biz.com/wp-content/uploads/2017/04/Using-Background-Music-to-Affect-the-Behavior-of-Supermarket-Shoppers.pdf).

Fit beats one-size-fits-all. Effects vary by audience and setting. A [meta-analysis of retail music studies](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0148296306000282) shows that outcomes depend on execution and context, not just on whether music is on or off.

The right music makes waiting easier. Music that matches the setting can [make a wait feel shorter](https://chaireomerdesserres.hec.ca/wp-content/uploads/2020/05/The-Impact-of-Music-on-Consumers-Reactions-to-Waiting-for-Services.pdf) and support friendlier behaviour in queues and lobbies.

Different people, different reactions. In the study's two retail tests, women more often preferred no music or slower music, and men more often preferred music and faster tempos. Short-term sales can rise even when some guests enjoy the visit less, which can cost repeat visits later [unless the mix is tuned to the audience](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0969698912000732).

structuredContent.value: Does this apply outside retail?

In many settings, yes. The experiments took place in an electronics store and a supermarket, but the same path from emotion to behaviour applies in other service venues. Earlier work found similar effects of music [in restaurants](https://www.jstor.org/stable/2489234) when the soundtrack fits the moment and the crowd, and the [PAD model](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0022435997900166) describes the same mechanism for any space.
The SensEar checklist for retail, bars and restaurants
Use it to test safely, without hurting the guest experience.

items: Set clear goals. Retail: more dwell time and bigger baskets, or faster quick trips. Bars: more orders per guest or faster table turns. Restaurants: control the pace of seating and upsells without raising stress.
Choose tempo by goal. For browsing and discovery, lean slower; for quick movement and faster turns, lean faster. Always test a middle set as your control.

Match the crowd and the time of day. Mornings and older or family-heavy periods: lighter, slower sets. Evenings and younger or high-energy periods: a notch faster. If your audience skews female, trial quieter or slower sets; if it skews male, trial more energetic ones. Check against your own footfall data.
Keep the volume comfortable. People should talk without raising their voice. If staff say they are tired by midday, it is too loud.
Keep the style on brand. Pick tracks that feel like your space; good fit beats raw BPM tweaks.
Measure short and long results. Short term: sales per visitor, time on site, orders per table, people leaving the queue. Long term: satisfaction, reviews, repeat rate, staff feedback.
Test, then tune. Run A/B dayparts for two weeks per set, change one variable at a time (tempo, volume or playlist), keep the winner and retest monthly.

structuredContent.value: How a wait feels can matter as much as how long it lasts
A wait that seems short to a manager can feel long to a guest when the room works against them.
Why waiting feels longer than it is

Customers often [overestimate how long they have waited](https://www.researchgate.net/profile/Ale-Smidts/publication/247220346_Effects_of_waiting_on_the_satisfaction_with_the_service_Beyond_objective_time_measures/links/5cc83a9e4585156cd7bc091c/Effects-of-waiting-on-the-satisfaction-with-the-service-Beyond-objective-time-measures.pdf), and satisfaction drops as the perceived wait grows. The usual fixes are operational and cut the actual queue time, but a [field study in a call centre](https://www.researchgate.net/profile/Naveen-Donthu/publication/242337184_Closing_the_gap_between_perceived_and_actual_waiting_times_in_a_call_center_Results_from_a_field_study/links/64bff61a8de7ed28bac2b9e0/Closing-the-gap-between-perceived-and-actual-waiting-times-in-a-call-center-Results-from-a-field-study-Results-from-a-field-study.pdf) shows that the setting and the information given during the wait also shape satisfaction, sometimes more than a few seconds or minutes saved.
How the environment shapes perception

The physical and sensory setting affects the emotional, cognitive and physiological responses that drive evaluations and behaviour. [Servicescape research](https://academic.oup.com/jcr/article-abstract/13/2/286/1846377) ties these effects to basic states of pleasure and arousal, which colour time perception and satisfaction.
The factors that matter

Lighting, temperature, music, scent and background noise [set the sensory baseline](https://academic.oup.com/jcr/article-abstract/13/2/286/1846377) and can shift satisfaction and perceived time in hospitality and retail.
Colour, furnishings, signage and layout [guide flow and expectations](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0278431918310430), and with them attention and mood during a wait.
Who is present matters too. [Staff and other guests nearby can soften the experience](https://philpapers.org/rec/PRUCRT), and waiting with others can make a longer wait easier to accept.
How music changes perceived wait time

[Music that puts people in a good mood tends to shorten a wait](https://chaireomerdesserres.hec.ca/wp-content/uploads/2020/05/The-Impact-of-Music-on-Consumers-Reactions-to-Waiting-for-Services.pdf), while poorly matched music can lengthen it. The mechanism combines attention, mood and tempo, which [influence our internal sense of time](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1071581921001749). What works for a given audience and setting has to be tested and curated, because [responses vary by genre, volume and tempo](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0022435997900166).
Practical steps for managers

Make the ambient conditions a management priority: set lighting, temperature, music volume and tempo for each space and each part of the day, then check the result against guest feedback and your own figures. Know the emotional profile of the music you choose for your guests, and use [playlists matched to the mood and pace](/services/signature-playlists/) of each zone and each kind of wait.
If your guests wait anywhere, the room they wait in is worth a listen. [Tell us which room](/contact/).

hero.title: What you need to know before we start
hero.subtitle: Our answers to the questions we hear most often from hotels, restaurants and bars.

items.question: Is it legal to play music from Spotify, YouTube or Apple Music in my business?
items.answer: Usually not. Consumer streaming platforms (Spotify Free or Premium, YouTube, Apple Music and so on) are licensed for personal use only, even on a paid subscription, so they do not cover public performance in a commercial space. Using them in a business can break copyright law and lead to fines. To play music legally to your guests, you need a service licensed for business use.

items.question: What is a public performance license, and why do I need it?
items.answer: A public performance licence makes sure artists, songwriters and publishers are paid when their music plays in a public space. Every restaurant, bar, hotel or shop that plays music needs one, and the venue pays for it to the collecting societies. SensEar does not issue or handle licences, but we explain what applies before you sign.

items.question: Is your music fully licensed?
items.answer: The music plays from a platform licensed for business use, so you are not playing from a personal streaming account. The public performance fees are paid separately by the venue to the Greek collecting societies, as they are for any business that plays music.

items.question: How much does it cost?
items.answer: It depends on the venue: how many zones it has, how many hours music plays and which service you need. The first call or visit is free of charge, and after the visit we send a written proposal with the cost, usually within 7 to 10 days.

items.question: How long does it take to create a custom playlist?
items.answer: Usually 1 to 2 weeks after the proposal is agreed.

items.question: Do you work outside Athens?
items.answer: Yes, across Greece. Our music plays today in venues in Athens, on Antiparos and on Sifnos, and we have curated an event on Paros.

items.question: Do you also do DJ sets for events?
items.answer: Yes, with Event Soundtracks: playlists and sets by our own DJs for one event, from the guests’ arrival to the last song, with a sound check. We visit the venue free of charge before we send our offer.

items.question: How is this different from a background music service?
items.answer: A background music service gives you ready-made playlists that thousands of other venues also use. We build the programme around your venue: your areas, your hours, and the way your day runs, and we keep it updated. The tracks are chosen by people who have heard them, not generated from a genre setting.

items.question: Can I update the music playlists myself?
items.answer: You don’t need to, and we generally advise against it. We handle the scheduling by hour and by area and the updates, and you can ask for changes at any time. Your staff can still adjust the volume on the spot.

items.question: How often does the music change?
items.answer: We suggest new music every month and a change of direction each season, at a rhythm agreed with you, so regular guests and your staff are not hearing the same tracks all year.

items.question: Do I need special equipment for playing your music playlists?
items.answer: A basic system is usually enough to start. If the room itself is the problem, we assess it, tell you what needs to change, and coordinate the specialist partners who carry out the work, then tune the result. See Audio Upgrades.

items.question: What happens if the internet goes down?
items.answer: The music keeps playing offline, on the same schedule in every zone. We manage the playlists remotely, so once the connection is back, any changes come through as usual.

items.question: Do you offer support after setup?
items.answer: Yes. We are available for ongoing support, updates, and any adjustments you need along the way. Just send us a message and we will talk about it.

items.question: What music should I play in my restaurant?
items.answer: It depends on the hour and on what you want to happen in the room. A slower tempo when you want guests to stay and enjoy the meal, a faster one when you need tables to turn, and always music that fits the character of the place. The key is that it changes through the day, from lunch to late evening. More in the article How music shapes buyer behaviour.

items.question: How can I improve the atmosphere of my venue with music?
items.answer: With three things: music that fits the character of the venue rather than the taste of whoever is on shift, a schedule that changes with the hours of the day and the zones, and a volume that lets people talk. Research shows that music that fits a space changes how guests perceive it, even how long a wait feels. See the article How spaces shape perceived wait time.

items.question: How loud should music be in a restaurant or bar?
items.answer: Loud enough to fill the room, but not so loud that people raise their voices to talk. If staff are tired by midday, it is too loud. A lot of noise even makes sweet and salty flavours in the food less noticeable. See the article Sonic seasoning: how sound changes taste.

items.question: Does music affect how long guests stay and how much they spend?
items.answer: In many cases, yes. Field studies in shops and restaurants found that slower music keeps guests longer and can lift spending, and in one restaurant chain brand-fit playlists brought revenues about 9.1% higher than random chart hits. Results depend on the audience and the venue, which is why the music should be chosen for yours. See the article How brand-fit music converts browsers into buyers.

intro.title: What Audio Upgrades cover
paragraphs: Audio Upgrades improve the sound in your venue from two sides: the sound system, meaning the speakers and where they are placed, and the acoustics of the room, such as echo or sound reaching the neighbours.

We start by listening to your specific problems and needs, and we write them down carefully. Then we visit with our partners in sound measurement, sound isolation and soundproofing, test what you already have and propose what needs to change.

Our partners supply the equipment and carry out the installation and acoustic work. We arrange every visit, supervise the work and run the final tuning, so you deal with one team and receive one invoice.

case_study.title: Music for the bar, quiet for the neighbours
paragraphs: In a bar in the centre of Athens, the music carried up to the neighbours on the floor above and out onto the street. The client also wanted a warmer, clearer sound with more bass, one that suits dance music as well as lounge and mid-tempo tracks, and lets guests talk easily even at high volume.
We visited with our partners in sound measurement, sound isolation and soundproofing, who ran their tests on site. The visit and the assessment were free.
The work is finished. The sound is now warmer and crystal clear, and it no longer disturbs the neighbours upstairs or the area around the bar.

intro.title: What Experience Design is
paragraphs: Experience Design is the planning and building of everything a guest meets in your venue.
That includes the website and booking, the arrival, the space, the light, the sound, the service and what happens after the visit.

Most venues design these parts separately, with different people and at different times. Guests notice when the parts do not fit. We look at the whole visit through the guest's eyes, find where it breaks, and design each touchpoint to support the same story.
We do not stop at a report. We stay with you until the new experience is part of your daily operation.

items.question: What is experience design for a hotel or restaurant?
items.answer: It is the design of everything a guest meets, from booking and arrival to service, space, sound and the contact after the visit, so that it all works as one whole.

items.question: How is it different from interior design or marketing?
items.answer: Interior design shapes the space, and marketing brings guests in. Experience design connects both with service and the senses, so the visit works well from start to finish.

items.question: Do we need to renovate?
items.answer: Usually not. Most changes are about service, timing, sound, light and small details. We suggest bigger changes only when their value is clear.

items.question: How long does a project take?
items.answer: An Experience Audit usually takes 2 to 3 weeks. A full project takes about 2 to 4 months, depending on the size of the venue.

items.question: Do you only work with hotels?
items.answer: No. We also work with restaurants, bars, retail stores, wellness spaces, cultural spaces and events.

items.question: Do you work outside Athens?
items.answer: Yes. We are based in Athens and work with venues across Greece and its islands.

items.question: Is music included?
items.answer: Sound is part of the sensory brief in every project. If you also want daily music for your venue, our Signature Playlists service covers it.

intro.title: The work comes first
intro.p1: In a gallery, or on a runway, what you are showing comes first. Sound is there to hold attention on it, not to compete for it, and the difference between the two is a few decibels or the wrong genre.
intro.p2: For the rooms, Signature Playlists keep a low, considered line through opening hours. For an opening, a preview or a show, Event Soundtracks plans the night, and where the room's own speakers flatten everything, Audio Upgrades brings in our partners for placement and acoustics.
